subtopics.title: Soil: The Living Skin That Feeds the Country

questions.question: Soil horizons are arranged, from the surface downward, as:
options: Dark humus-charged topsoil, paler subsoil, weathered rock, then solid parent material
Solid rock, subsoil, topsoil, then humus
Humus, parent rock, subsoil, then topsoil
Sand, clay, gravel, then bedrock in equal bands

questions.question: Soil is treated as non-renewable on a human timescale because:
options: No new soil has formed anywhere since the last ice age
Building a few centimetres of topsoil can take several hundred years, while one storm on bare ground can strip more than that in an afternoon
Soil minerals cannot be replaced by weathering
Only volcanic regions can form new soil

questions.question: South Africa's arable endowment amounts to roughly:
options: Half the country arable, a quarter high-potential
A third arable, a tenth high-potential
12 per cent arable, with scarcely 3 per cent genuinely high-potential
2 per cent arable, none of it high-potential

questions.question: Vegetation acts as the soil's bodyguard because:
options: Plants absorb eroded soil through their leaves
Tall grass hides the soil from the wind entirely
Roots pump water out of the topsoil before storms
Leaves absorb the punch of falling raindrops, roots lace the crumbs together, and litter feeds the binding humus

subtopics.title: Causes of Soil Erosion: Human, Animal and Physical

questions.question: The escalating sequence of water erosion runs:
options: Splash, then sheet, then rill, then gully
Gully, then rill, then sheet, then splash
Sheet, then splash, then gully, then rill
Rill, then gully, then splash, then sheet

questions.question: The crucial nuance about physical causes is that:
options: They operate only in deserts
Physical agents usually complete what land use begins — bare ground is the precondition, and bare ground is almost always manufactured
They are entirely absent in South Africa
Wind and water never act on the same field

questions.question: The apartheid homeland system is a past cause of erosion because it:
options: Banned contour ploughing nationwide
Removed all livestock from the reserves
Packed too many people and livestock onto the smallest, poorest land, engineering the overuse that still scars the former Transkei and Ciskei
Subsidised chemical fertilisers too heavily

questions.question: Trampling contributes to erosion because:
options: Hooves fertilise the grass excessively
Cattle eat the soil directly along their paths
Trampled soil absorbs too much water
Compacted stock paths stop rain soaking in, so water runs off — and the daily route to the drinking point often becomes a future gully's first channel

subtopics.title: Evidence and Effects Across South Africa

questions.question: Evidence of soil erosion carved into the South African landscape includes:
options: Dongas through the Eastern Cape, the Thukela basin and Sekhukhune, rivers running brown after storms, and dams losing storage to silt
Expanding forests across the Karoo
Falling river sediment loads everywhere
Deepening topsoil on communal lands

questions.question: The Hazelmere Dam on the Mdloti River illustrates:
options: A dam destroyed by flooding
Siltation so severe that engineers had to raise the dam wall to win back storage the sediment had swallowed
The first dam built specifically to trap sediment
A reservoir unaffected by upstream erosion

questions.question: The effects of erosion on people include:
options: Cheaper food as farming intensifies
Longer dam lifespans and better water security
Falling yields and farm incomes, collapsing rural livelihoods and migration, silt-shortened dam life, and costly fertiliser replacing free fertility
Guaranteed harvests through irrigation

questions.question: Erosion is called a disaster in slow motion because:
options: It only happens over geological ages
It moves at exactly the speed of a glacier
Every storm involved makes national headlines
No single storm makes the news, yet the accumulating loss undermines food security, water security and rural livelihoods all at once

subtopics.title: Management, and the GIS Toolkit for Soil

questions.question: Contour ploughing prevents erosion because:
options: Furrows laid along the slope's contour lines act as miniature dams instead of downhill drains
It buries the topsoil below plough depth
It doubles the speed of runoff harmlessly
It removes the need for any vegetation cover

questions.question: Gabions control gully erosion by:
options: Sealing the gully with poured concrete
Tripping floodwater so it slows and drops its sediment, gradually raising the gully floor until grass can anchor it
Diverting the river into a neighbouring valley
Pumping the floodwater back upslope

questions.question: Spatial resolution and spectral resolution describe, respectively:
options: The satellite's altitude and its speed
The number of images per day and their file size
The ground size of one pixel, and the wavelength bands the sensor records — with infrared exposing bare or stressed ground early
The map scale and the printing quality

questions.question: Correctly matched GIS data types are:
options: A river as a point, a borehole as an area, a field as a line
A catchment as a line, a fence as a point, a gully head as an area
All features stored only as areas
A gully head as a point, a river as a line, and an erosion-risk zone as an area

subtopics.title: The Bank Account That Fills by Teaspoons

questions.question: Teaspoon deposits, bucket withdrawals summarises the fact that:
options: Soil builds over centuries but a single storm on bare ground can remove decades of accumulation in an afternoon
Farmers measure fertiliser in teaspoons
Rivers deposit more soil than they remove
Soil forms fastest during thunderstorms

questions.question: The ten-plates picture of South Africa says that:
options: Ten per cent of food is imported each year
Only about one plate in ten stands on arable land, with just a corner truly first-class — and sixty million people eat from it
Every province grows enough food for itself
Ten dams supply all irrigation water

questions.question: Every cause of erosion collapses into the sentence:
options: The rain always wins in the end
Rivers are the enemies of farmers
Somebody, somehow, fired the bodyguard — the vegetation that protected the soil was removed
Wind and water take turns by season

subtopics.title: How a Footpath Becomes a Canyon

questions.question: The five acts of the erosion script run:
options: Overgrazing bares a patch, raindrops splash particles loose, sheetwash shaves the surface, rills form, and the rills merge into a donga
A donga opens, rills follow, then sheetwash, then splash, then overgrazing
Wind lifts sand, cattle arrive, grass grows, rain falls, rocks split
Ploughing, planting, harvesting, resting, flooding

questions.question: Many dongas were born as footpaths because:
options: Footpaths are always dug below ground level
The daily stock route to water is beaten hard as a floor, refuses to absorb rain, and becomes the original drain that concentrates runoff
Walkers carry soil away on their shoes
Paths are deliberately routed through wet ground

questions.question: Wind erosion on dry, bare fields:
options: Removes coarse sand first and leaves the fine grains
Only occurs on coastal dunes
Lifts the finest, most fertile grains first and abandons the coarse sand — the Dust Bowl plot of the 1930s
Deposits fertile dust evenly over the same field

questions.question: History plays a part in South Africa's erosion script because:
options: Colonial railways compacted the entire interior
Early farmers refused to keep livestock
The country's climate was wetter before 1900
The homeland map squeezed people and cattle onto the smallest, weakest land, so the deepest dongas today run through those former districts

questions.question: The prevention stitches for croplands include:
options: Contour ploughing, mulch and stubble as a winter blanket, and crop rotation to re-set the humus glue
Deeper ploughing straight down the slope
Burning stubble immediately after every harvest
Leaving fields bare so the sun can sterilise them

questions.question: For grazing land, the stitches are:
options: Doubling the herd to fertilise the veld faster
Carrying only what the veld can feed — its carrying capacity — and rotating the herd so every pasture rests
Concentrating all animals on one sacrificial camp
Replacing all cattle with crops immediately

questions.question: The national teams working the needle include:
options: Working for Coal and the Weather Bureau
The roads agency and the postal service
LandCare sewing farm-level stitches, Working for Water uprooting thirsty alien trees, and Working on Fire guarding the green cover
Only private insurance companies

questions.question: The menders choose where to stitch first by:
options: Waiting for farmers to report every gully by post
Stitching provinces in alphabetical order
Treating the flattest land first in all cases
Stacking slope, rainfall and soil layers in a GIS — with infrared betraying bare ground from orbit — to reveal where risk concentrates
